period: Predynastic to the Arab conquest, c. 5000 BC - AD 641
summary: Three thousand years of pharaohs fit one simple rhythm: three strong 'Kingdoms', with messy 'Intermediate Periods' in between.
look: This is the mental shelf on which every other entry sits: whenever a label says '18th Dynasty' or 'Ptolemaic', come back here to place it. On this trip, Giza is Old Kingdom, Luxor and Abu Simbel are New Kingdom, and the river temples of Edfu, Kom Ombo, Esna and Philae are Greek and Roman. Islamic Cairo begins with the Arab conquest of 641.
story:
Egyptologists still use the list of 30 dynasties drawn up in the 3rd century BC by Manetho, an Egyptian priest writing in Greek for the Ptolemies. Modern historians grouped them into 'Kingdoms', when one king ruled the whole Nile valley, and 'Intermediate Periods', when the country split. Exact dates are still argued over; those below are the conventional ones.

Before about 3100 BC, farming villages along the Nile grew into two rival kingdoms, Upper Egypt in the south and Lower Egypt in the Delta. Narmer is the first king we know who claimed both. After the Early Dynastic Period (Dynasties 1-2) came the Old Kingdom (Dynasties 3-6, 2686-2181 BC), the pyramid age, ruled from Memphis. A long reign, over-mighty governors and drought brought the First Intermediate Period.

Mentuhotep II reunited Egypt from Thebes around 2055 BC, opening the Middle Kingdom, the classical age of literature. In the Second Intermediate Period the Hyksos, rulers from western Asia, held the Delta until Ahmose drove them out around 1550 BC. That began the New Kingdom (to 1069 BC): Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Akhenaten, Tutankhamun, Ramesses II, and nearly everything you will see in Luxor.

Then power fragmented: priest-kings in Thebes, Libyan and Nubian pharaohs, an Assyrian sack of Thebes in 663 BC, a Saite revival, two spells of Persian rule. Alexander arrived in 332 BC; the Greek dynasty of his general Ptolemy ended with Cleopatra in 30 BC, and Rome took over. Christianity slowly replaced the old gods, and the Arab conquest of 641 opened the chapter you will meet in Islamic Cairo on the 16th.
details: Memory trick: Old Kingdom = pyramids, Middle Kingdom = literature and worried faces, New Kingdom = Luxor's temples and tombs.
Giza on the 12th is Dynasty 4. Abu Simbel on the 17th is Dynasty 19. Edfu on the 20th is Ptolemaic.
Siwa's oracle temple (13-15 Oct) is Late Period, the place Alexander came to consult Amun in 331 BC.
Dates marked 'c.' on labels are estimates: for the early dynasties they can be off by decades or more.
fun_fact: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.
narration: Think of this as the shelf where every other story sits. Ancient Egyptian history runs for about 3,000 years, and the trick is a simple rhythm: three strong Kingdoms, with messy Intermediate Periods in between. Before about 3100 BC, villages along the Nile grew into two rival kingdoms, south and north. Narmer is the first king we know who claimed both. Then comes the Old Kingdom, from about 2686 to 2181 BC, the age of the pyramids you will walk around at Giza on the 12th. Drought and greedy governors broke it apart. Around 2055 BC a Theban king, Mentuhotep the Second, put Egypt back together and began the Middle Kingdom, the classical age of poems and careworn royal faces. Next, foreign rulers called the Hyksos took the north, until Ahmose expelled them around 1550 BC. That opens the New Kingdom, the age of Hatshepsut, Tutankhamun and Ramesses the Great, and of almost everything you will see in Luxor and at Abu Simbel. After 1069 BC, power splinters: priest kings, Libyans, Nubians, Persians. Alexander arrives in 332 BC, his general Ptolemy founds a Greek dynasty, and it ends with Cleopatra in 30 BC, when Rome takes over. The river temples of Edfu, Kom Ombo and Philae belong to that last chapter. So keep this in your pocket: pyramids old, Luxor new, river temples Greek.

summary: Five centuries when Egypt's kings were living gods able to raise mountains of stone, ending in drought and famine.
look: You meet the Old Kingdom at Giza on the 12th and in the museums' earliest galleries. Recognise its art by calm, broad-shouldered, muscular figures staring straight ahead, fists clenched, left foot striding forward: Khafre with the falcon behind his head, Rahotep and Nofret, the wooden Ka-aper.
story:
The capital was Memphis, near modern Cairo, and the king was a god on earth who could command the labour of the whole country. Under Djoser, first king of Dynasty 3, his official Imhotep stacked stone platforms into the Step Pyramid at Saqqara. Sneferu, founder of Dynasty 4, built at least three pyramids, at Meidum and Dahshur, and moved more stone than any other king, perfecting the true pyramid by trial and error. His son Khufu, grandson Khafre and great-grandson Menkaure built Giza. The workers were not slaves but rotating crews of farmers and skilled specialists, housed and fed in a town beside the plateau.

Dynasty 5 spent less on pyramids and more on sun temples for Ra at Abusir, and sent ships to Punt for incense. Its last king, Unas, was the first to have the Pyramid Texts, Egypt's oldest religious writings, carved inside his burial chamber.

In Dynasty 6, provincial governors made their posts hereditary and grew rich. Pepi II reigned for more than 60 years (later tradition said over 90) and outlived his heirs; then a drought in the 22nd century BC failed the Nile floods. The tomb of the governor Ankhtifi describes famine stalking the land.
details: Old Kingdom statues: broad shoulders, long torso, visible muscles, fists clenched, left foot forward, eyes fixed far away.
Late in Dynasty 6 the style changes: shoulders narrow, muscles soften and eyes grow larger. A quick way to date a statue.
At Giza, the rows of flat-topped mastaba tombs around the pyramids belong to officials buried beside their king.
The king was not yet called 'pharaoh': that word, 'great house', became a title for the king himself only in the New Kingdom.
fun_fact: Sneferu, Khufu's father, moved more stone than his famous son: he needed three attempts, at Meidum and Dahshur, to get the pyramid right.
narration: The Old Kingdom is the age of the pyramids, roughly 2686 to 2181 BC, Dynasties 3 to 6, ruled from Memphis just south of Cairo. Its kings were living gods, and they could summon the whole country to build. It starts with Djoser, whose official Imhotep stacked stone platforms into the Step Pyramid at Saqqara. Then Sneferu, founder of Dynasty 4, learned by trial and error, building at least three pyramids and moving more stone than any other king. His son Khufu, grandson Khafre and great grandson Menkaure built Giza. The workers were not slaves: they were farmers on rota and skilled crews, fed and housed in a town beside the plateau. Later kings spent their money on sun temples for Ra, and the last king of Dynasty 5, Unas, carved the first Pyramid Texts inside his tomb. Then local governors grew rich, a very long reign left no clear heir, and a drought failed the floods. The age ended in famine. In the museum, spot Old Kingdom statues by their broad shoulders, calm faces and the left foot striding forward.

period: Middle Kingdom, Dynasties 11-12 (and early 13), c. 2055-1650 BC
summary: After a century of chaos, kings from Thebes rebuilt Egypt and left its classic literature and its most human royal faces.
look: You meet the Middle Kingdom in faces: Senusret III's heavy-lidded, worried portraits and Mentuhotep II's black-skinned seated king. In Luxor, the White Chapel of Senusret I in Karnak's open-air museum and Mentuhotep's terraced temple at Deir el-Bahari belong to it, and so do the governors' tombs of Sarenput I and II on the hill at Aswan.
story:
Mentuhotep II took the Theban throne in 2055 BC, defeated the rival kings of Herakleopolis and spent years reuniting the country; he reigned 51 years. Amenemhat I, probably the vizier of the last Mentuhotep and not of royal birth, founded Dynasty 12 and moved the capital north to a new city, Itjtawy, 'Seizer of the Two Lands', near el-Lisht. He was probably murdered in a palace plot, the event that opens the Story of Sinuhe.

To avoid such crises, Dynasty 12 kings made their sons co-regents. Senusret I pushed into Nubia and built the White Chapel at Karnak. Senusret III campaigned brutally in Nubia and built massive mud-brick forts at the Second Cataract; Greek writers later remembered him as the conqueror Sesostris. Amenemhat III turned the Faiyum's marshes into farmland. The line ended with Sobekneferu, the first securely attested woman to rule as king.

Later Egyptians treated this as their classical age. Scribes copied its stories for centuries: Sinuhe the courtier in exile, the Eloquent Peasant, the Shipwrecked Sailor. Officials now painted the old royal spells, the Coffin Texts, inside their own coffins, and pilgrims flocked to Osiris at Abydos.
details: Senusret III's portraits: heavy eyelids, hollow cheeks, big ears. Often read as a king feeling the weight of office.
The White Chapel of Senusret I in Karnak's open-air museum (22nd): Middle Kingdom carving at its crispest.
Block statues, a man squatting wrapped in his cloak like a cube, became popular in this period: spot them in any museum.
Mentuhotep II's temple at Deir el-Bahari (21st), beside Hatshepsut's, was the model she copied five centuries later.
fun_fact: The Story of Sinuhe was a school classic: hundreds of years after it was written, apprentice scribes were still copying it onto pottery shards.
narration: The Middle Kingdom is Egypt's classical age, about 2055 to 1650 BC. After the Old Kingdom collapsed, a Theban king, Mentuhotep the Second, fought the rival rulers of the north and put the country back together. He reigned for 51 years. The kings who followed, called Amenemhat and Senusret, moved the capital north and ruled father and son together to avoid civil war. They pushed deep into Nubia, built huge forts at the Second Cataract, and drained the Faiyum for farmland. Greek writers later remembered one of them, Senusret the Third, as the conqueror Sesostris. This is the age of the great stories: Sinuhe, the courtier who fled into exile, and the Shipwrecked Sailor, marooned on an island with a giant talking snake. Scribes copied them for centuries. Look at the royal portraits of this time: heavy eyelids, hollow cheeks, big ears. Senusret the Third looks tired and worried, a king who knows the job is hard. In Luxor on the 22nd, find the White Chapel of Senusret the First at Karnak, as crisp as the day it was carved.

summary: Five centuries of empire, when Thebes grew rich on gold and tribute and built most of what you will see in Luxor and at Abu Simbel.
look: Most of the second half of this trip is New Kingdom: Karnak and Luxor temples, the Valley of the Kings, Hatshepsut's terraces, Abu Simbel, the Ramesseum, Medinet Habu, and Tutankhamun's treasure at the GEM. Recognise it by bright colour, chariots, slender elegant figures, and cartouches of Thutmose, Amenhotep and Ramesses everywhere.
story:
It began with a war of liberation. Theban kings fought the Hyksos who ruled the Delta, and around 1550 BC Ahmose drove them out and chased them into Canaan. The lesson Egypt learned was to keep enemies far away. Thutmose I became the first pharaoh to cross the Euphrates. Hatshepsut ruled as king and sent ships to Punt. Thutmose III fought about 17 campaigns and held an empire from Syria deep into Nubia. Under Amenhotep III, tribute and Nubian gold made Egypt the richest state of its day. His son Akhenaten replaced the gods with the Aten; Tutankhamun restored them, and the general Horemheb erased the whole episode.

Horemheb chose his vizier as heir, and Ramesses I founded Dynasty 19. Seti I and Ramesses II fought the Hittites, famously at Kadesh, where both sides claimed victory; they later signed a peace treaty. Ramesses built from the Delta to Abu Simbel and put his name on older kings' statues too.

In Dynasty 20, Ramesses III beat back the Sea Peoples in his eighth year, but wars drained the treasury. In his 29th year the royal tomb-builders of Deir el-Medina staged the first recorded strike when their rations failed, and he died in a harem plot. Eight more kings called Ramesses watched power drift to the High Priests of Amun while robbers emptied the royal tombs.

Throughout, Thebes was the religious capital. Kings were buried in hidden tombs in the Valley of the Kings, with mortuary temples out on the plain, and poured their spoils into Amun's house at Karnak. In this age 'pharaoh', literally 'great house', became a word for the king himself.
details: Chariots and horses came into use around the Hyksos period; New Kingdom battle walls at Karnak and Abu Simbel are full of them.
Tomb hidden in the valley, temple public on the plain: that split is why the West Bank has both (21st).
Ramesses II often recarved older kings' statues with his own name: look for cartouches cut deeper than the rest.
The royal mummies of this age, Ramesses II among them, are at NMEC in Fustat, not at the GEM.
fun_fact: History's first recorded strike happened here, in Ramesses III's 29th year, when the royal tomb-builders' grain rations failed to arrive.
narration: The New Kingdom, about 1550 to 1069 BC, is the Egypt of empire and gold, and most of what you will see in Luxor and at Abu Simbel. It begins with a war of liberation. Foreign kings called the Hyksos held the north, until a Theban prince, Ahmose, drove them out. Egypt learned to keep its enemies far away. Thutmose the First marched to the Euphrates. Hatshepsut ruled as king and sent ships to the incense land of Punt. Thutmose the Third fought about 17 campaigns and built an empire from Syria to deep inside Nubia. With Nubian gold and Asian tribute, Amenhotep the Third lived like a sun king. His son Akhenaten threw out the old gods for a single sun disc, and Tutankhamun brought them back. Then the Ramesside kings took over. Seti the First and Ramesses the Second fought the Hittites at Kadesh, both sides claimed victory, and they later signed a peace treaty. Ramesses the Third held off the Sea Peoples, but money ran short, and the royal tomb builders went on the first recorded strike when their bread did not arrive. Through it all, Thebes was the holy city. Kings were buried in the Valley of the Kings and poured their spoils into Amun's temple at Karnak. When you see a cartouche on the 21st or 22nd, try to read Thutmose, Amenhotep or Ramesses.

period: Third Intermediate and Late Periods, 1069-332 BC
summary: Seven centuries of priest-kings, Libyan chiefs, Nubian pharaohs and Persian emperors: Egypt divided, invaded, and still building.
look: You meet this age in odd corners: the silver coffin of Psusennes from Tanis in the Cairo museums, Taharqa's single standing column in Karnak's first court, Amun's oracle temple at Siwa, and the kiosk of Nectanebo I at Philae. Its art often copies the Old Kingdom on purpose, so check the label before guessing a statue's date.
story:
After Ramesses XI died, Egypt split, politely: kings ruled the north from Tanis in the Delta while the High Priests of Amun governed the south from Thebes, and the two families intermarried. At Tanis in 1939-40 Pierre Montet found intact royal burials, including Psusennes I in a silver coffin.

Around 945 BC Shoshenq I, of Libyan descent, reunited Egypt and raided Palestine, listing the towns on a Karnak gateway. His successors split into rival lines. Around 732 BC Piye of Kush marched north and founded Dynasty 25 of Nubian pharaohs; Taharqa built at Karnak. Assyria invaded and sacked Thebes in 663 BC.

Psamtik I of Sais reunited the country with the help of Greek and Carian mercenaries and ruled 54 years. Saite kings revived Old Kingdom art, and Amasis courted the Greek world. In 525 BC the Persian Cambyses conquered Egypt; Herodotus tells of an army he sent against Siwa that vanished in a sandstorm. Egypt broke free in 404 BC, and Nectanebo I and II, the last native pharaohs, built furiously until Persia returned in 343 BC. In 332 BC the Persian governor handed Egypt to Alexander without a fight.
details: Karnak's first court (22nd): the one tall column still standing belongs to the kiosk of Taharqa, a Nubian pharaoh.
Saite statues copy Old Kingdom style, smooth and idealised: some look 2,000 years older than they are.
Siwa (13-15 Oct): the oracle temple at Aghurmi dates to this age, usually credited to Amasis of Dynasty 26.
Philae (18th): the first building you reach is the kiosk of Nectanebo I, built by the last native dynasty.
Animal mummies boomed in this age: cats, ibises and crocodiles offered by pilgrims fill museum cases.
fun_fact: In the 590s BC, Greek mercenaries marching south for Psamtik II scratched their names on a leg of one of Abu Simbel's colossi: some of the oldest dated Greek graffiti anywhere.
narration: After the New Kingdom, Egypt spent seven centuries divided, invaded and still building. From about 1069 BC, kings ruled the north from Tanis in the Delta, while the High Priests of Amun ruled the south from Thebes. Then came pharaohs of Libyan descent, like Shoshenq, who raided Palestine and listed the towns he took on a gateway at Karnak. Around 732 BC, Piye of Kush marched north from Nubia and founded a dynasty of Nubian pharaohs. The Assyrians threw them out and sacked Thebes in 663 BC. Psamtik of Sais rebuilt Egypt with Greek mercenaries, and his dynasty copied Old Kingdom art so faithfully that their statues can look 2,000 years older than they are. In 525 BC the Persian king Cambyses conquered Egypt, and Herodotus tells how one of his armies vanished in the sand on its way to Siwa. The last Egyptian born pharaohs, the Nectanebos, built at Philae and Karnak until Persia returned. Then, in 332 BC, Alexander walked in. At Karnak, look for the single tall column of the Nubian king Taharqa, alone in the first court.

period: Ptolemaic and Roman Egypt, 332 BC - AD 641
summary: For three centuries Macedonian Greeks ruled as pharaohs and built the river temples you will visit, before Rome made Egypt its granary.
look: From the 18th to the 20th you walk through this age: Philae, Kom Ombo, Edfu and Esna are all Ptolemaic or Roman. Recognise it by walls crowded with small, rounded, fleshy figures, columns with elaborate floral capitals, and cartouches that spell Greek names like Ptolemaios and Kleopatra sound by sound. The Greek layer is everywhere: Edfu was Apollonopolis, Aswan was Syene, Esna was Latopolis.
story:
Alexander took Egypt from the Persians in 332 BC, was hailed as son of Amun at Siwa, founded Alexandria and left, never to return alive. After his death in 323 BC his general Ptolemy held Egypt, diverted Alexander's body to be buried there, and in 305 BC made himself king. Every male heir was called Ptolemy; the queens were Cleopatras, Arsinoes and Berenices, and from Ptolemy II they married their siblings, Egyptian-style.

The Ptolemies ran a two-level country. Greeks lived under Greek law, and Alexandria, with its Library and Museum, became the intellectual capital of the Mediterranean: Euclid and Eratosthenes worked there. For the Egyptian majority the kings played pharaoh, funding temples to win over the powerful priests. Ptolemy III began Edfu on 23 August 237 BC; the main temple was finished in 212 BC, the whole complex only in 142 BC. The Rosetta Stone of 196 BC is one such priestly decree, honouring Ptolemy V in hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek.

Cleopatra VII, by Plutarch's account the only one of her line to learn Egyptian, staked everything on Caesar, then Mark Antony. After defeat at Actium she and Antony killed themselves in Alexandria in 30 BC, and Octavian took Egypt as his personal possession. Emperors appear on temple walls dressed as pharaohs, Egypt shipped grain to Rome, and the Fayum mummy portraits show its mixed Greek-Egyptian middle class.

Christianity spread from the 3rd century. The last hieroglyphic inscription was carved at Philae in AD 394, Isis's temple there was closed under Justinian around 537, and the Arab conquest of 641 ended the Roman chapter.
details: Cartouches at Edfu and Kom Ombo spell Greek names sound by sound: look for the lion, which stands for L in Ptolemy and Cleopatra.
At Esna and Philae, Roman emperors offer to the gods in a pharaoh's kilt and crown, named in hieroglyphs as 'Caesar'.
Philae (18th): near the Gate of Hadrian is the last known hieroglyphic inscription, dated AD 394.
Ancient tourists left Greek graffiti on many walls; at Philae, Christians later carved crosses into the reliefs.
fun_fact: Eratosthenes of Alexandria measured the Earth's circumference using the sun's angle at Syene, which is Aswan, where you will be on the 18th.
narration: For the last three centuries before Christ, Egypt's pharaohs were Greeks. Alexander the Great took the country from the Persians in 332 BC, visited the oracle of Amun at Siwa, founded Alexandria, and left. When he died, his general Ptolemy kept Egypt and made himself king. Every one of his male heirs was called Ptolemy, the queens were Cleopatras, Arsinoes and Berenices, and from the second generation they married their own siblings, like Egyptian gods. The Ptolemies lived as Greeks in Alexandria, with its Library and its scholars, but to the Egyptian priests they played pharaoh. They paid for huge new temples in the old style: Edfu, Kom Ombo, Esna and Philae, the places you will walk through from the 18th to the 20th. The last of the line, Cleopatra the Seventh, was said to be the only one who bothered to learn Egyptian. She allied with Julius Caesar, then Mark Antony, lost to Octavian at Actium, and died in 30 BC. Rome took Egypt as its granary, and the emperors had themselves carved on temple walls in pharaoh's kilts. Christianity slowly closed the temples, and the last hieroglyphs were cut at Philae in 394 AD. On any Ptolemaic wall, look inside the cartouche for a lion: it is the letter L, in Ptolemy or Cleopatra.

summary: Egyptian texts name more than 1,400 gods, but about twenty do most of the work, and you can tell them apart by their heads and hats.
look: Gods fill every temple and tomb wall: usually a human body in a kilt or a long dress, with an animal head or a headdress that works like a name badge. Most hold an ankh in one hand and a sceptre in the other. Read the head first, then the crown, then the short column of hieroglyphs above the figure that gives the name.
story:
The Egyptologist James Allen counts more than 1,400 named deities. Most began as local gods, and as towns merged into a kingdom, priests arranged them into families. The most influential was the Ennead, 'the Nine', of Heliopolis, now under north-east Cairo. The creator Atum, identified with the sun god Ra, rose from the dark waters of Nun onto the first mound and produced Shu, air, and Tefnut, moisture. They had Geb, the earth, and Nut, the sky. Geb and Nut had four children: Osiris, Isis, Seth and Nephthys. Horus, son of Isis and Osiris, completes the family and its great drama.

Other cities had their own systems. Memphis said Ptah created the world by conceiving it in his heart and speaking it with his tongue, and paired him with the lioness Sekhmet and their son Nefertem. Thebes, where you will spend the 21st and 22nd, built its family around Amun, his wife Mut and their son, the moon god Khonsu. Hermopolis had eight primeval gods, the Ogdoad.

Egyptians did not treat these accounts as rivals. Gods could merge, as Amun-Ra or Ra-Horakhty, and borrow each other's crowns, so Isis wears Hathor's horns. The animal head is not a portrait but a statement of character: the falcon soars like the sky, the jackal prowls the cemetery, the lioness is dangerous.
details: Falcon head: Horus, often in the double crown. Falcon head with a sun disc and cobra: Ra or Ra-Horakhty.
Jackal: Anubis. Ibis or baboon: Thoth. Ram with long wavy horns: Khnum. Crocodile: Sobek. Lioness: Sekhmet.
Two tall plumes and blue skin: Amun. Tight skullcap and mummy body: Ptah. Mummy body, white crown with feathers: Osiris.
Cow horns around a sun disc: Hathor, or Isis borrowing them. Small throne on the head: Isis.
Front-facing dwarf with tongue out: Bes. Pregnant hippo standing upright: Taweret.
fun_fact: The hieroglyph for 'god' is not a face but a flag on a pole, like the giant flagstaffs that once stood in the grooves of every temple gateway.
narration: Egyptian texts name more than 1,400 gods, but you only need about twenty, and you can recognise them like playing cards: by the head and the hat. The core family comes from Heliopolis, now under north Cairo. There, the creator Atum, a form of the sun god Ra, rose from the dark waters onto the first mound of earth. He produced Shu, the air, and Tefnut, moisture. They had Geb, the earth, and Nut, the sky. Geb and Nut had four children: Osiris and Isis, Seth and Nephthys. Seth murdered Osiris, and Horus, son of Isis, avenged him. That family drama is behind half the walls you will see. Other cities had their own teams. In Memphis, Ptah the craftsman created the world by speaking it. In Thebes, where you go on the 21st, the family is Amun, his wife Mut and their son, the moon god Khonsu. Gods could also merge, so Amun and Ra become Amun Ra, king of the gods. Now the cheat sheet. Falcon head: Horus. Jackal: Anubis. Ibis: Thoth. Ram: Khnum. Crocodile: Sobek. Lioness: Sekhmet. Two tall feathers: Amun. Cow horns around a sun disc: Hathor, or Isis borrowing them. Green skin and a mummy body: Osiris. On the next wall you see, name the first god by the head alone.

period: Attested from the Pyramid Texts, c. 2350 BC, to Plutarch, c. AD 100
summary: A murdered king, a widow who would not give up, and a son who fought 80 years for the throne: the story that let every Egyptian hope to live again.
look: You will see this story in pieces everywhere: Isis and Nephthys kneeling as kites at either end of a mummy on its bier, Anubis bending over the body, Horus with his harpoon. At Edfu on the 20th, Horus spears Seth as a tiny hippo on the inner west wall, and Philae's temple of Isis is built on her side of the tale.
story:
No Egyptian text tells the whole story. Egyptians avoided writing out a god's death, since words could make things real. We piece it together from the Pyramid Texts, hymns and healing spells, a bawdy New Kingdom tale called 'The Contendings of Horus and Seth', and, most fully, the Greek writer Plutarch around AD 100.

Osiris ruled Egypt as a good king until his brother Seth killed him. In Plutarch's version Seth and 72 accomplices made a splendid chest to Osiris's exact size and offered it at a banquet to whoever fitted inside. Osiris lay down, the lid was nailed shut and sealed with lead, and the chest was thrown into the Nile. It drifted to Byblos in Lebanon, where a tree grew around it and the king made the trunk a pillar of his palace. Isis found it and brought the body home; Seth, hunting by moonlight, found it again and cut it into 14 pieces. Isis recovered all but the phallus, eaten by fish, and made a replacement.

With Nephthys, Anubis and Thoth, Isis reassembled Osiris: the first mummy. Hovering as a kite, she fanned breath into him and conceived Horus, whom she hid in the Delta marshes. Osiris went on to rule the dead.

Grown up, Horus challenged Seth before the gods. In 'Contendings' the case drags on for 80 years, through boat races, hippo fights and Seth tearing out Horus's eye, until Horus wins. So every king was Horus alive and Osiris dead, and in time every Egyptian could become 'the Osiris' too.
details: Isis and Nephthys at the head and foot of a mummy, often as winged women or kites: the mourning scene on coffins and tomb walls.
Edfu, inner face of the west enclosure wall (20th): Horus harpoons Seth, shrunk to a hippo small enough to be harmless.
The djed pillar, Osiris's backbone, echoes the palace pillar at Byblos that hid his coffin in Plutarch's version.
Isis seated with the baby Horus on her lap: thousands of bronze figurines of the scene fill museum cases.
fun_fact: Because Osiris drowned in the Nile, Egyptians treated anyone who drowned in the river as sacred.
narration: This is the story behind half of what you will see in Egypt: a murder, a widow who would not give up, and a son's revenge. Osiris was a good king. His jealous brother Seth wanted the throne. In the Greek version told by Plutarch, Seth built a beautiful chest to Osiris's exact size and offered it at a banquet to whoever fitted inside. Osiris lay down, the lid slammed shut, and the chest was thrown into the Nile. It floated all the way to Byblos in Lebanon, where a tree grew around it and became a pillar in the king's palace. Isis, his wife and sister, tracked it down and brought him home. Seth found the body again and cut it into 14 pieces. Isis searched the whole country, found every piece but one, which a fish had eaten, and with her sister Nephthys, Anubis and Thoth, wrapped him back together. Osiris became the first mummy. Isis, as a kite, fanned breath into him and conceived their son Horus, then hid the baby in the marshes. Osiris went down to rule the dead. Horus grew up and fought Seth for 80 years, losing an eye and winning the throne. So every king was Horus in life and Osiris in death, and in time every Egyptian hoped to become an Osiris too. Look for Isis and Nephthys kneeling at the two ends of a mummy: that is this story.

period: Attested from c. 2350 BC; king of the gods from c. 1550 BC
summary: A minor god whose name means 'the hidden one' rode Thebes' rise to become king of the gods, and his priests ended up ruling half of Egypt.
look: Amun is the man with blue skin and two tall straight plumes on a flat crown, often seated on a throne. His animals are the ram with curled horns, lining Karnak's avenue as sphinxes, and the goose. You will meet him on almost every wall in Luxor on the 21st and 22nd, sometimes with chisel scars where Akhenaten's agents hacked out his figure.
story:
His name, Imen, means something like 'the hidden one'; a Pyramid Text addresses the god 'whose name is unknown'. He first appears in the pyramid of Unas around 2350 BC, one of eight primeval gods of Hermopolis and possibly a god of the wind. Under Dynasty 11 he replaced the war god Montu as patron of Thebes, and Senusret I began his temple at Karnak.

When Theban kings expelled the Hyksos, they credited Amun. Merged with the sun as Amun-Ra, 'king of the gods', he received the spoils of empire, and Karnak became one of the largest religious complexes ever built. At the Opet festival his statue sailed from Karnak to Luxor Temple. Ordinary people prayed to him too: workmen at Deir el-Medina called him the god 'who comes at the voice of the poor'. He absorbed the ram god of Nubia and the fertile Min.

Wealth made his priests dangerous. Akhenaten closed his temples and erased his name; Tutankhamun restored him. By the end of the New Kingdom, Amun's priests held about two thirds of all temple land and 90 percent of the ships, and from 1080 BC High Priests such as Herihor and Pinedjem ruled the south as kings in all but name.

Greeks knew him through his desert oracle at Siwa and called him Zeus Ammon, with ram's horns. In 331 BC the oracle greeted Alexander as Amun's son, and coins struck by his successors show Alexander wearing the horns.
details: Two tall plumes on a flat crown: Amun. The same crown on a stiff ithyphallic figure with a raised flail: Amun-Min.
Karnak's ram-headed sphinxes (22nd) are Amun as a ram, each sheltering a small figure of the king between its paws.
His wife Mut wears a vulture headdress under the double crown; their son Khonsu has a youth's sidelock and a moon disc.
Siwa (13-15 Oct): the oracle temple at Aghurmi is where Alexander put his question to Amun.
fun_fact: Amun lives on in chemistry and geology: ammonia comes from 'sal ammoniac', salt linked to his temple in the Libyan desert, and ammonite fossils are named for his ram's horns.
narration: Amun is the god with blue skin and two tall feathers on his crown, and Luxor is his city. His name means the hidden one. He began as a minor god of air, one of eight primeval gods, until about 2000 BC, when he became the patron of Thebes. Then Thebes won. When Theban princes drove out the Hyksos around 1550 BC, they thanked Amun, merged him with the sun god as Amun Ra, king of the gods, and poured the treasure of an empire into his house at Karnak. Every year his statue sailed in a golden boat from Karnak to Luxor Temple for the Opet festival. He was not only for kings. Workmen in the tomb builders' village prayed to him as the god who comes at the voice of the poor. His wealth made his priests powerful. Akhenaten closed his temples and chiselled out his name. Tutankhamun brought him back. By the end of the New Kingdom, his priests held about two thirds of all temple land, and the High Priests of Amun ruled southern Egypt like kings. The Greeks met him at the oracle of Siwa and called him Zeus Ammon, with ram's horns. When Alexander visited in 331 BC, the oracle greeted him as Amun's son. At Karnak, look at the avenue of ram headed sphinxes: each ram is Amun, guarding a little king between its paws.
